```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

These examples reconstruct the current state from event counts and use it in
the baseline function `mu`. Fosset's spread model disables narrowing at the
minimum spread; the queue model makes departures proportional to the number
of visitors present. Each model defines its own specification and simulated data.

See the [examples overview](extended_example.html) for other model topics.

```{r}
library(emhawkes)
```

## Fosset's state-dependent spread model {#fosset-spread-model}

Fosset, Bouchaud and Benzaquen (2020),
[Endogenous Liquidity Crises](https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-5468/ab7c64),
Section 4.1, equations (8a)--(8b), model spread widening and narrowing as two
event types. Let $N_+$ and $N_-$ count these events and let the spread, in ticks, be

$$
S(t) = S_0 + N_+(t) - N_-(t).
$$

Their linear model has predictable intensities

$$
\lambda_+(t) = \nu_+ + a\int_{[0,t)} b e^{-b(t-s)}\,dN_+(s),
\qquad
\lambda_-(t) = \nu_-\,\mathbf{1}_{\{S(t-)\ge 2\}}.
$$

Only widening events excite future widening. Narrowing is disabled at a one-tick
spread. We use $\nu_+,\nu_-$ for the paper's $\lambda_0^+,\lambda_0^-$ and
$a,b$ for its $\alpha,\beta$. The package's `alpha[1, 1]` is therefore $ab$;
$a$ is the integrated excitation, not the jump size. The other `alpha` entries
are fixed zeros. Both event types have unit marks.

The example uses positive rates, $0<a<1$, and an explicit zero initial excitation.
This restricts the example to a Hawkes-stable widening process. A stationary
spread additionally requires $\nu_+/(1-a)<\nu_-$. The values below are chosen
for a stationary-spread illustration. The nonlinear models later in the paper
are separate specifications.

Define `mu`, `alpha`, and `beta` directly, then construct the `hspec` object.
Rows identify affected event types, and columns identify triggering event types.
Log rates enforce positivity, and a logit parameter enforces $0<a<1$.
The shared name `log_b` keeps the same decay parameter in `alpha` and `beta`.

```{r fosset-specification}
spread0_fosset <- 1

mu <- function(param = c(log_nu_plus = log(1), log_nu_minus = log(3)), n, N) {
  previous_event <- max(1L, n - 1L)
  spread <- spread0_fosset + N[previous_event, 1] - N[previous_event, 2]
  matrix(c(exp(param[["log_nu_plus"]]),
    exp(param[["log_nu_minus"]]) * (spread >= 2)), nrow = 2)
}

alpha <- function(param = c(logit_a = qlogis(0.4), log_b = log(2))) {
  jumps <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  jumps[1, 1] <- plogis(param[["logit_a"]]) * exp(param[["log_b"]])
  jumps
}

beta <- function(param = c(log_b = log(2))) {
  matrix(exp(param[["log_b"]]), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
}

h_fosset <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)
```

For the baseline callback, `N[n - 1, ]` describes the state before event `n`.
The same callback is called with `n + 1` after the jump, so the narrowing rate
changes immediately when the spread reaches or leaves one tick.

```{r fosset-simulation}
set.seed(20261018)
path_fosset <- hsim(h_fosset, size = 4001, lambda_component0 = 0)
spread_fosset <- spread0_fosset + path_fosset$N[, 1] - path_fosset$N[, 2]
stopifnot(all(spread_fosset >= 1),
  all(path_fosset$lambda[c(spread0_fosset, head(spread_fosset, -1)) == 1, 2] == 0),
  all(path_fosset$rambda[spread_fosset == 1, 2] == 0))
plot(path_fosset$arrival, spread_fosset, type = "s",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Spread (ticks)")
```

Estimate all four model parameters from a different starting point. The example
uses R's stats optimizer and the default numerical gradient. Automatic engine
selection uses the supported C++ likelihood; simulation of this count-dependent
baseline uses the R path. No analytic Jacobians are required. Change the default
`param` vectors to choose fitting starting values, then create a second `hspec`.

```{r fosset-fit}
formals(mu)$param <- c(log_nu_plus = log(0.7), log_nu_minus = log(2.5))
formals(alpha)$param <- c(logit_a = qlogis(0.25), log_b = log(1.2))
formals(beta)$param <- c(log_b = log(1.2))
start_fosset <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)
fit_fosset <- hfit(start_fosset,
  inter_arrival = path_fosset$inter_arrival, type = path_fosset$type,
  lambda_component0 = 0, optimizer = "stats", method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 500, reltol = 1e-10))
theta_fosset <- coef(fit_fosset)
estimated_fosset <- c(
  nu_plus = exp(theta_fosset[["log_nu_plus"]]),
  nu_minus = exp(theta_fosset[["log_nu_minus"]]),
  a = plogis(theta_fosset[["logit_a"]]),
  b = exp(theta_fosset[["log_b"]]))
cbind(true = c(nu_plus = 1, nu_minus = 3, a = 0.4, b = 2),
  estimated = estimated_fosset)
fit_diagnostics(fit_fosset)$status
fit_diagnostics(fit_fosset)$computation$engine
```

The estimated coefficients are on the log/logit scale. Parameter recovery varies
between realizations; inspect convergence and uncertainty rather than expecting
exact recovery from a single path.

There is an independent check for the narrowing rate. If $T_{\mathrm{open}}$ is the
time spent with $S\ge2$, its log-likelihood contribution is
$N_-(T)\log\nu_- - \nu_- T_{\mathrm{open}}$. Its maximum is
$\widehat{\nu}_- = N_-(T)/T_{\mathrm{open}}$.
The observation window ends at the last supplied event.

```{r fosset-check}
open_time_fosset <- sum(path_fosset$inter_arrival[-1] *
  (head(spread_fosset, -1) >= 2))
c(fitted = estimated_fosset[["nu_minus"]],
  independent = sum(path_fosset$type == 2) / open_time_fosset)
restored_fosset <- fitted_hspec(fit_fosset)
replay_fosset <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = restored_fosset,
  inter_arrival = path_fosset$inter_arrival, type = path_fosset$type,
  infer = TRUE), fit_initial_state(fit_fosset)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(logLik(fit_fosset)),
  unname(replay_fosset$loglikelihood), tolerance = 1e-8)))
```

## A Hawkes/M/infinity queue: website visits and departures {#hawkes-infinite-server}

Daw and Pender (2018),
[Queues Driven by Hawkes Processes](https://doi.org/10.1287/stsy.2018.0014),
Section 3, define a Hawkes/PH/infinity queue. With one exponential service phase,
their model is a Hawkes/M/infinity queue. Interpret arrivals as website visits
and service completions as departures. Every visitor starts service immediately;
$Q(t)$ counts all visitors still present in the system.

Let $N_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{out}}$ count visits and departures. With
initial population $Q_0$ and zero initial excitation, the model is

$$
Q(t) = Q_0 + N_{\mathrm{in}}(t) - N_{\mathrm{out}}(t),
$$

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{in}}(t)
= \nu + a\int_{[0,t)} e^{-b(t-s)}\,dN_{\mathrm{in}}(s),
\qquad
\lambda_{\mathrm{out}}(t) = \delta Q(t-).
$$

Here $\nu$ is the arrival baseline, $a$ is the jump in arrival intensity, $b$ is
its decay rate, and $1/\delta$ is the mean service time. In the paper's notation,
these are $\lambda^*$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, and the single-phase service rate.
Unlike the normalized kernel in the preceding spread example, this kernel has
jump size $a$ and integrated excitation $a/b$.

The arrival process is an autonomous Hawkes process. The population affects the
departure intensity, while an arrival's contribution to future arrivals continues
to decay after that visitor leaves. This is exactly the single-phase special
case of the paper's queueing model.

Define the three components and construct the `hspec` object directly. Log
parameters keep all four rates positive, and the function-valued `alpha` keeps its three
structural zeros fixed during estimation. The example uses $a<b$ for a stable
arrival process; the log parameterization alone does not enforce that inequality.

```{r hawkes-queue-specification}
q0_queue <- 0

mu <- function(param = c(log_nu = log(0.4), log_delta = log(0.8)), n, N) {
  previous_event <- max(1L, n - 1L)
  population <- q0_queue + N[previous_event, 1] - N[previous_event, 2]
  matrix(c(exp(param[["log_nu"]]),
    exp(param[["log_delta"]]) * population), nrow = 2)
}

alpha <- function(param = c(log_a = log(0.5))) {
  jumps <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  jumps[1, 1] <- exp(param[["log_a"]])
  jumps
}

beta <- function(param = c(log_b = log(1.2))) {
  matrix(exp(param[["log_b"]]), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
}

h_queue <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)
```

Event type 1 is a visit and event type 2 is a departure. The baseline callback
reads `N[n - 1, ]` to obtain the population before event `n`. After the event it
is called with `n + 1`, so the departure rate changes immediately. When $Q=0$,
the departure rate is zero without a separate boundary correction.

```{r hawkes-queue-simulation}
set.seed(884102)
path_queue <- hsim(h_queue, size = 6001, lambda_component0 = 0)
population_queue <- q0_queue + path_queue$N[, 1] - path_queue$N[, 2]
population_before_queue <- c(q0_queue, head(population_queue, -1))
stopifnot(all(population_queue >= 0),
  all(population_before_queue[path_queue$type == 2] > 0),
  all(path_queue$rambda[population_queue == 0, 2] == 0))
```

For a readable view, plot the first 400 events. `rambda` contains the intensity
immediately after each event, so its second column equals $\delta Q(t)$.

```{r hawkes-queue-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5, dev.args=list(bg="white"), fig.alt="Step plots of visitors present and departure intensity over time; departure intensity is proportional to the current visitor count."}
local({
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1), mgp = c(2.5, 0.8, 0))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  shown <- seq_len(min(401L, length(path_queue$arrival)))
  plot(path_queue$arrival[shown], population_queue[shown], type = "s",
    xlab = "Time", ylab = "Visitors present")
  plot(path_queue$arrival[shown], path_queue$rambda[shown, 2], type = "s",
    xlab = "Time", ylab = "Departure intensity")
})
```

Estimate the four rates from both arrival and departure times. This uses the
stats optimizer with numerical differentiation. Simulation uses the R event
loop for the state-dependent baseline; automatic likelihood selection supports
the C++ engine for this observed-count callback.

```{r hawkes-queue-fit}
formals(mu)$param <- c(log_nu = log(0.3), log_delta = log(1.1))
formals(alpha)$param <- c(log_a = log(0.3))
formals(beta)$param <- c(log_b = log(0.9))
start_queue <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)
fit_queue <- hfit(start_queue,
  inter_arrival = path_queue$inter_arrival, type = path_queue$type,
  lambda_component0 = 0, optimizer = "stats", method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 500, reltol = 1e-10))
theta_queue <- coef(fit_queue)
estimated_queue <- c(
  nu = exp(theta_queue[["log_nu"]]),
  delta = exp(theta_queue[["log_delta"]]),
  a = exp(theta_queue[["log_a"]]),
  b = exp(theta_queue[["log_b"]]))
cbind(true = c(nu = 0.4, delta = 0.8, a = 0.5, b = 1.2),
  estimated = estimated_queue)
fit_diagnostics(fit_queue)$status
```

The likelihood factorizes into an arrival contribution and a departure
contribution. Over the observation window ending at the last supplied event,
the latter is, up to parameter-independent terms,

$$
N_{\mathrm{out}}(T)\log\delta
- \delta\int_0^T Q(t)\,dt.
$$

Thus $\widehat\delta=N_{\mathrm{out}}(T)/\int_0^T Q(t)\,dt$ provides an independent
check of the fitted service rate. Restore the fitted specification and replay
the same data to check that its likelihood is preserved.

```{r hawkes-queue-check}
person_time_queue <- sum(path_queue$inter_arrival[-1] * head(population_queue, -1))
c(fitted = estimated_queue[["delta"]],
  independent = sum(path_queue$type == 2) / person_time_queue)
restored_queue <- fitted_hspec(fit_queue)
replay_queue <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = restored_queue,
  inter_arrival = path_queue$inter_arrival, type = path_queue$type,
  infer = TRUE), fit_initial_state(fit_queue)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(logLik(fit_queue)),
  unname(replay_queue$loglikelihood), tolerance = 1e-8)))
```

This example starts with `q0_queue = 0`. For a nonempty initial system, set
`q0_queue` before defining `mu` and keep it fixed through simulation and fitting.
Initial population and initial Hawkes excitation are distinct:
`q0_queue` counts visitors already present, while `lambda_component0` describes the
remaining excitation from arrivals before the observation window.
